title: The Bishop's Candlesticks
text:
Jean Valjean had served nineteen years in the galleys, five for stealing a loaf of bread for his sister's starving children and the rest for trying to escape. When he was finally released, his yellow passport marked him as a dangerous ex-convict. In the town of Digne every inn turned him away, and even a dog kennel would not have him.

At last he knocked at the door of the bishop, Monseigneur Myriel. The bishop welcomed him as a guest, called him monsieur, sat him at his table and served him by the light of two silver candlesticks, using the silver plates he kept for company. In the night Valjean, hardened by years of brutality, stole the silver plates and fled.

In the morning gendarmes brought him back. They had caught him with the silver. The bishop greeted Valjean warmly. "I am glad to see you. But I gave you the candlesticks too. They are silver like the rest. Why did you not take them with the plates?" The gendarmes released him. The bishop gave him the candlesticks and said quietly that he must not forget his promise to use the silver to become an honest man. "Jean Valjean, my brother, you no longer belong to evil, but to good. I am buying your soul."

Valjean had made no such promise. Shaken, he left the town and wandered in turmoil, and after one last petty theft that horrified him, he broke down weeping. He went on to live an honest life, and he kept the candlesticks until he died.
lesson: Mercy offered where punishment is expected can change a person in ways punishment rarely does. Treat people as who they could become.
source: Victor Hugo, Les Miserables (1862), Part One, Book Two
